Music in the Bible
MYOO-zik in the BY-bul
noun phrase (the biblical doctrine of music)
From “music” (Greek mousike); the biblical treatment of music—its instruments, its place in worship and life, and its God-given power.

Biblical Definition

Music in the Bible is the whole biblical treatment of music—its instruments, its place in worship and in life, and its God-given power over the soul. Scripture is full of music. The Psalter calls for praise “with the sound of the trumpet… with the psaltery and harp… with the timbrel and dance… with stringed instruments and organs”; David appointed Levites as singers and players for the temple worship; and music attended the great moments of redemption—the song of Moses at the Red Sea, the songs of Zion, the new song of the redeemed in glory. The apostle bids the church sing “psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord.” The dictionary marks music as a good gift of God, given for His praise and for the gladdening of the human heart, with real power to move the affections—a power Scripture both honours (David's harp soothing Saul's troubled spirit) and treats soberly. It holds the biblical doctrine of music against opposite errors. The first is the asceticism that distrusts music as worldly or dangerous and would banish it—a denial of a gift God Himself commanded for His worship. The second is the modern abuse that makes music an end in itself, prizing performance, entertainment, and emotional manipulation over the truth sung and the God praised—letting the melody trample the words, or using music's power to work up feelings mistaken for the Spirit. In worship, music is governed by the regulative principle and the rule that it serve the word richly, the song teaching and admonishing in the truth. The dictionary commends music as a servant—of the praise of God and the good of the soul—neither despised as evil nor idolized as an end, but received as a gift and used to the glory of the Giver.

Webster 1828 Definition

The biblical treatment of music—its instruments, its place in worship and life, and its God-given power (Psalm 150; Ephesians 5:19); a good gift for God's praise and the heart's gladness, against both ascetic distrust and the modern abuse that makes it an end in itself.

Key Scripture

Ps 150:3 — "Praise him with the sound of the trumpet: praise him with the psaltery and harp."

Ps 150:4 — "Praise him with the timbrel and dance: praise him with stringed instruments and organs."

Eph 5:19 — "Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;"

1 Ch 16:9 — "Sing unto him, sing psalms unto him, talk ye of all his wondrous works."

Modern Corruption

One error is the asceticism that distrusts music as worldly and would banish it; the other is the modern abuse that makes music an end in itself, prizing performance and emotional manipulation over the truth sung.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is music as a good gift of God, servant of His praise and the soul's good. The first corruption is the asceticism that distrusts music as worldly or dangerous and would banish it from worship and life. The dictionary answers from the Psalter, which commands praise with trumpet, harp, timbrel, and strings, and from David, who appointed Levites to sing and play in the temple. Music is no enemy of godliness but a gift God Himself commanded for His worship, with power to gladden the heart and even, as David's harp soothed Saul, to quiet the troubled spirit.

The opposite and more modern corruption makes music an end in itself—prizing performance, entertainment, and emotional effect over the truth sung and the God praised. It lets the melody trample the words, fills worship with the vacant and the self-centred, and uses music's real power over the affections to work up feelings mistaken for the moving of the Spirit. The dictionary holds music to its proper place: a servant, not a master. In worship it is governed by the regulative principle and must serve the word richly, the song teaching and admonishing in the truth. Music is neither to be despised as evil nor idolized as an end, but received as a gift and used—in worship and in life—to the glory of the Giver.

Hebrew Roots

From the Greek mousike (the art of the Muses) and the rich biblical vocabulary of song and instrument; music as a gift of God for praise and gladness, governed in worship by the regulative principle.

Mousike, Greek, the art of music.

The Psalter's many instruments: trumpet, harp, psaltery, timbrel, strings, organs.

David's appointment of Levitical singers and players for the temple.

Music's power over the soul (David's harp and Saul, 1 Samuel 16:23).

In worship, governed by the regulative principle and made to serve the word.

Usage

"The pastor honoured music as a gift of God against the asceticism that would banish it."

"He warned that worship-music must serve the word, not trample it for performance and effect."

"She used music's power to gladden the heart and praise the Giver, not to manufacture feeling."
